title: The Nile: A River of Life
summary: How the Nile forms from two branches, flows north through the desert, once flooded every year to leave rich soil, builds a delta, and changed after the Aswan High Dam.
poll: Stopping the Nile's yearly flood was a good idea.

versions.title: The Long River
versions.text:
The Nile is a big river. It is in Africa. It is very, very long. It runs north. It ends at the sea.

The Nile has two main parts. One is the White Nile. It starts near a big lake. One is the Blue Nile. It starts in the hills. The two meet. Then they flow as one.

Most land by the Nile is desert. It is hot. It is dry. But the land by the river is green. Most of the folks in Egypt live there.

Long ago, the Nile had a flood each year. Rain fell far off. The river rose. It spread on the land. Then it went down. It left dark soil. Farmers grew wheat in it.

At the end, the river splits. It makes a delta. The land there is green, too.

Now a big dam holds the water back. There is no flood. The dam makes power. But the dark mud stays back at the dam. So farmers must feed the soil.

The Nile gives us water. We must keep it clean.

versions.title: The Nile: A River of Life
versions.text:
The Nile is a mighty river in Africa. It is one of the longest rivers in the world, about 6,650 kilometers long. Unlike many rivers, it flows north. It ends at the Mediterranean Sea.

The Nile has two main arms. The White Nile begins in the region around Lake Victoria. The Blue Nile begins at Lake Tana, high in the mountains of Ethiopia. The two arms join in the city of Khartoum in Sudan. From there, they travel north as one river.

Much of the land along the Nile is desert. It gets almost no rain. Yet a narrow strip of land beside the water is green. That is why most people in Egypt live close to the river.

For thousands of years, the Nile had a flood every summer. Heavy rains fell in the Ethiopian hills. The river rose and covered the fields. When the water went down, it left a layer of dark mud. This mud made the soil rich. Farmers planted wheat in it. The ancient Egyptians even named their land "the black land."

Close to the sea, the Nile splits into many streams. They spread out in a fan shape called a delta. The delta is full of farms.

In 1970, Egypt finished the Aswan High Dam. It holds back the water in a huge lake. Now there is no flood. The dam also makes power. But the mud stays in the lake. So farmers must add plant food to the soil.

The Nile still gives millions of people water to drink. Keeping it clean is very important.

The two branches join at the city of Khartoum, in Sudan, and continue north as one river. Its strong current carries the water all the way to the sea.

Much of the land along the lower Nile is desert, where rain almost never falls. Yet the narrow valley beside the water is green and fertile. For this reason, nearly all of Egypt's people live within a short distance of the river.

For thousands of years, the Nile flooded every summer. Heavy rains fell on the Ethiopian highlands, and the Blue Nile rushed downstream. The river spread across the fields, and when it went down, it left a layer of dark silt. This silt made the soil rich, so farmers could plant wheat and other crops. The ancient Egyptians called their land "the black land" because of it.

The river also helped people travel. Boats floated north with the current. To go south, sailors raised their sails, because the wind usually blows from the north.

Near the sea, the Nile divides into smaller streams that spread out in a fan shape called a delta. In 1970, Egypt completed the Aswan High Dam, which stores water in Lake Nasser. The dam stopped the floods and produces electricity. However, the silt now stays behind the dam, so farmers must add plant food to their fields. Keeping the river clean is still important for everyone who depends on it.

The Nile is among the most celebrated rivers on Earth. Stretching approximately 6,650 kilometers across northeastern Africa, it is one of the longest rivers in the world, and, unusually, it flows from south to north before eventually emptying into the Mediterranean Sea.

The river is formed by two principal branches, each fed by a network of smaller streams known as tributary rivers. The White Nile originates in the region surrounding Lake Victoria, in the heart of the continent, while the Blue Nile emerges from Lake Tana in the mountainous highlands of Ethiopia. The two branches unite at the city of Khartoum, in Sudan, and continue northward as a single river whose steady current transports the water through several countries.

Much of the territory along the lower Nile is desert, where rainfall is extremely rare. Nevertheless, the narrow valley beside the water remains remarkably green and productive. Consequently, nearly the entire population of Egypt lives within a short distance of the river, depending on it for drinking water, agriculture, and transportation.

For thousands of years, the Nile flooded every summer. Heavy seasonal rains drenched the Ethiopian highlands, and the Blue Nile carried the additional water downstream. The river spread across the surrounding fields, and when it gradually retreated, it deposited a layer of dark sediment called silt. This sediment enriched the soil, allowing farmers to cultivate wheat and other crops, and they dug canals for irrigation so that water could reach fields farther from the banks. The ancient Egyptians even called their country "the black land" because of this dark, fertile earth.

The river also functioned as a natural highway. Boats drifted north with the current, while sailors traveling south raised their sails, because the prevailing wind usually blows from the north.

Near the coast, the Nile divides into smaller channels that spread out in a triangular fan called a delta. In 1970, Egypt completed the Aswan High Dam, which stores water in an enormous reservoir named Lake Nasser. The dam ended the destructive floods and generates electricity for homes and industries. However, the sediment is now trapped behind the dam, so farmers must apply fertilizer to replace the nutrients the floods once delivered. Protecting the river from pollution therefore remains essential for the millions of people who depend on it.

versions.title: The Nile: A River of Life
versions.text:
The Nile River stretches approximately six thousand six hundred fifty kilometers, flowing from south to north before finally emptying into the Mediterranean Sea, an orientation that distinguishes it from many of the world's other major rivers. Two principal branches combine to form this waterway: the White Nile, originating in the region surrounding Lake Victoria, and the Blue Nile, which begins at Lake Tana in the Ethiopian highlands; the two branches converge at Khartoum, in present-day Sudan, before continuing northward as a single river.

Beyond the narrow strip of fertile land bordering its banks, the surrounding landscape remains largely desert, a stark contrast that underscores just how essential the river has long been to human settlement in the region. Historically, the Nile flooded predictably each summer, depositing a layer of nutrient-rich sediment across the surrounding fields, a natural fertilizer so vital to agriculture that the fertile land it created became known simply as the black land. Farmers subsequently developed irrigation canals to extend the reach of this water supply well beyond the river's immediate banks.

The Nile also served as a vital artery for transportation long before modern infrastructure existed. Boats could drift northward with the river's natural current, then raise sails to travel southward against it, propelled instead by prevailing northern winds. This was an elegant natural solution that enabled trade and travel in both directions along the river's considerable length. Near the coast, the river fans out into numerous channels forming the Nile Delta before finally reaching the sea.

The completion of the Aswan High Dam in 1970 fundamentally altered the river's behavior. The resulting reservoir, Lake Nasser, brought the historic annual floods to an end while simultaneously providing valuable hydroelectric power. This same dam, however, now traps the sediment that once naturally fertilized farmland downstream, meaning farmers must increasingly rely on commercial fertilizer to replace what the river no longer provides naturally. Protecting the Nile from pollution remains essential, given how many millions of people continue to depend on its waters for their daily lives.

Even the smallest tributary feeding into the Nile's two main branches ultimately contributes to the volume of water and sediment that once sustained agriculture across the entire length of the river before the Aswan High Dam fundamentally changed that balance.

Few rivers illustrate so clearly how a single waterway can simultaneously sustain agriculture, transportation, and, through engineering projects like the Aswan High Dam, electricity generation.

versions.title: The Nile: A River of Life
versions.text:
The Nile River extends across approximately six thousand six hundred fifty kilometers, flowing from south to north before ultimately discharging into the Mediterranean Sea, an orientation that distinguishes it rather notably from many of the world's other major rivers. Two principal tributary branches combine to constitute this waterway: the White Nile, originating within the region surrounding Lake Victoria, and the Blue Nile, which originates at Lake Tana in the Ethiopian highlands; these two branches converge at Khartoum, within present-day Sudan, before continuing northward as a single unified river channel.

Beyond the comparatively narrow strip of fertile land bordering its banks, the surrounding landscape remains predominantly desert, a stark contrast that underscores precisely how indispensable the river has historically proven to sustained human settlement throughout the region. Historically, the Nile flooded predictably each summer, depositing an extensive layer of nutrient-rich sediment across the surrounding agricultural fields, a natural fertilizing agent so vital to successful cultivation that the fertile land it consistently created became known simply as the black land. Farmers subsequently developed elaborate irrigation canals specifically to extend the reach of this water supply considerably beyond the river's immediate banks.

The Nile additionally served as a vital artery for transportation long before the advent of modern infrastructure. Boats could drift northward utilizing the river's natural current, then raise sails to travel southward against that same current, propelled instead by prevailing northern winds, an elegant natural solution that enabled trade and travel in both directions along the river's considerable length. Nearer the coast, the river fans outward into numerous distinct channels forming the Nile Delta before finally discharging into the sea.

The completion of the Aswan High Dam in 1970 fundamentally and irreversibly altered the river's natural behavior. The resulting reservoir, Lake Nasser, brought the historic annual floods to a definitive end while simultaneously providing considerable hydroelectric power generation capacity. This same dam, however, now traps the sediment that previously fertilized farmland situated downstream, meaning that farmers must increasingly rely upon commercial fertilizer to substitute for what the river no longer naturally provides. Protecting the Nile from pollution consequently remains essential, given the many millions of people who continue to depend directly upon its waters for their daily sustenance and livelihood.

Even the smallest tributary stream feeding into either of the Nile's two principal branches ultimately contributes, however modestly, to the overall volume of water and sediment that once sustained agricultural productivity across the entire navigable length of the river before the Aswan High Dam fundamentally and permanently altered that long-established natural balance, a change whose consequences farmers downstream continue to manage today.

questions.stem: In the article, the word fertile describes land that...
options: is covered by sand
is always under water
is very far away from any river
can grow many healthy crops
questions.why: The green, fertile valley is where farmers grow crops, unlike the dry desert.

wrong.A: Sandy land is the desert, which is the opposite of fertile.
wrong.B: Fertile land was covered only during the flood, not always.
wrong.C: The fertile land is right beside the river.

questions.stem: Why could sailors use the same river to travel both north and south?
options: The river changes direction every night.
The current carried them north; the wind pushed their sails south.
Workers on the shore pulled the boats both ways with long ropes.
The dam pushed the water both ways.
questions.why: The river flows north, while the wind usually blows from the north, so sails could carry boats south.

wrong.C: The article does not describe pulling boats with ropes.
wrong.D: The dam holds water back; it does not push it both ways.

questions.stem: What is one problem the Aswan High Dam created for farmers?
options: Their fields now flood twice a year instead of once.
They no longer have any water.
The silt is trapped, so they must add plant food.
The river stopped reaching the sea.
questions.why: The article says the silt stays behind the dam, so the fields no longer get it and farmers must add plant food.

wrong.B: The dam stores water; farmers still have water.
wrong.D: The article does not say the river stopped reaching the sea.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe the floods before describing the dam?
options: To show how the river changed over time
To prove that the dam is older than the floods
To explain how to build a dam
To list the countries the river passes
questions.why: The author moves from the old yearly floods to the dam so readers can see what changed and why.

wrong.B: The floods came first, for thousands of years.
wrong.C: The article does not explain how dams are built.
wrong.D: The order of these parts is about time, not a list of countries.

MID.prompt: Explain one good result and one problem that came from the Aswan High Dam.
checklist: I named one good result of the dam.
I named one problem the dam caused.
I used details from the article to explain each one.
MID.modelAnswer: One good result of the Aswan High Dam is that it stopped the Nile's unpredictable summer floods and now produces electricity for the country. However, the dam also caused a problem: the silt that used to flow with the current and make the soil fertile now stays trapped behind the dam instead of reaching the fields. Because of this, farmers must add plant food to their land to replace the nutrients the river used to bring them.

keyWords.definition: a smaller river or stream that flows into a bigger river
keyWords.example: The little tributary added its water to the main river after the spring rains.

keyWords.definition: sand, mud, and tiny bits of rock carried by water and left in a new place
keyWords.example: A layer of sediment settled at the bottom of the glass of muddy water.

keyWords.definition: bringing water to fields through pipes or canals so crops can grow
keyWords.example: Drip irrigation helps farmers in dry places save water.

keyWords.definition: a large lake, often made by people, where water is stored
keyWords.example: The city fills its reservoir in winter so there is water in summer.

keyWords.definition: a material added to soil to help plants grow
keyWords.example: The gardener added fertilizer to help the roses bloom.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: The Nile's flow, floods, and sediment shaped where and how people in Egypt could live and farm.
The Aswan High Dam was a complete mistake.
The Nile is the only river in all of Africa that flows from south to north.
The White Nile supplies all of the Nile's water.
questions.why: The article traces how the river's water and sediment supported farming and settlement, and how that changed with the dam.

wrong.B: The article gives both benefits and costs of the dam, not a one-sided judgment.
wrong.C: The article calls the northward flow unusual but does not say it is the only one.
wrong.D: The article says heavy rains swelled the Blue Nile, so the White Nile is not the only source.

questions.stem: According to the article, what is a tributary?
options: The fan-shaped land where a river meets the sea
A canal dug to carry water to distant fields
A smaller stream that adds water to a larger river
A lake that stores water behind a dam
questions.why: The article describes networks of smaller streams contributing water to the main channel as tributaries.

wrong.D: That describes a reservoir such as Lake Nasser.

questions.stem: Why did ancient communities build canals for irrigation?
options: To drain the river before the flood
To carry water to fields farther from the riverbanks
To let boats sail south against the strong northern wind
To keep sediment out of their fields
questions.why: The article says canals let water reach fields located farther from the riverbanks.

wrong.A: The canals spread water; they did not empty the river.
wrong.C: Boats used sails and wind to go south, not canals.
wrong.D: Farmers wanted sediment because it enriched the soil.

questions.stem: What is Lake Nasser?
options: The source of the Blue Nile
A shallow lake in the delta near the Mediterranean Sea
The reservoir held back by the Aswan High Dam
The lake where the two branches meet
questions.why: The article states that the Aswan High Dam stores water in a reservoir named Lake Nasser.

wrong.A: The Blue Nile emerges from Lake Tana.
wrong.B: The article does not place Lake Nasser in the delta.
wrong.D: The branches meet at Khartoum, not in a lake.

questions.stem: Which detail from the article best supports the idea that the Nile was once a transportation route?
options: The river is about 6,650 kilometers long.
Farmers grew wheat on the land that the floods covered each summer.
Boats rode the current north and used the wind to sail south.
The river divides into channels near the coast.
questions.why: Describing how boats moved in both directions shows the river was used for travel.

wrong.A: Length alone does not show the river was used for travel.
wrong.D: This describes the delta's shape, not travel.

questions.stem: Based on the article, why might modern farming along the Nile cost more than ancient farming?
options: Modern farmers must buy fertilizer the floods once made unnecessary.
Modern farmers must pay high prices to ship their crops south by boat.
Modern farmers grow crops only in the desert.
Modern farmers have no access to river water.
questions.why: Because sediment is trapped behind the dam, farmers apply commercial fertilizer, an extra cost the floods once covered for free.

wrong.B: The article does not mention shipping costs.
wrong.C: Farming still happens in the river valley and delta.
wrong.D: The dam stores water, so farmers still have access to it.

questions.stem: How did the Aswan High Dam change life compared with the time of the yearly floods?
options: It made the floods much larger, although they came less often than before.
It ended the floods and added electricity, but kept sediment from reaching fields.
It moved the delta farther south.
It made the Blue Nile flow into Lake Victoria.
questions.why: The article lists both the benefits (no floods, hydroelectric power) and the cost (trapped sediment).

wrong.A: The article says the dam eliminated the floods.
wrong.C: The article does not say the delta moved.
wrong.D: The branches still flow north to meet at Khartoum.

questions.stem: What is the author's main purpose in the final paragraph?
options: To argue that dams should be removed
To describe the ancient boats in detail
To list every country the river crosses on its way to the sea
To weigh the dam's good and bad effects on the river
questions.why: The last paragraph explains what the dam gave and what it took away, then ends by stressing the need to protect the river.

wrong.A: The author never argues for removing the dam.
wrong.B: Boats are discussed in an earlier paragraph.
wrong.C: The final paragraph does not list countries.

HIGH.prompt: Was building the Aswan High Dam worth it? Explain your opinion using at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
checklist: I stated a clear opinion about the dam.
I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I mentioned a point on the other side and answered it.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I believe building the Aswan High Dam was worth it. The dam created a reservoir at Lake Nasser that stores water and generates electricity, and it also stopped the unpredictable floods that could threaten farmland and towns along the river. Some people might argue the dam hurt agriculture because the sediment that naturally made the soil fertile now stays trapped behind it, but farmers have adapted by using fertilizer and irrigation to keep their crops healthy. Overall, the dam's steady water supply and power are worth more than the cost of replacing the lost sediment.
